Unassuming 1972 Pontiac Ventura Hides a Nasty Surprise Under the Hood
18 photos
Photo: Mecum Auctions
Introduced in 1960 as a full-size car, the Pontiac Ventura was originally a custom trim package on the Catalina. Its success inspired Pontiac to join the personal luxury market with the Grand Prix in 1962. In 1971, Pontiac reassigned the Ventura to the compact market, where it remained through 1977.
Pontiac first joined the compact car market in 1961 with the Tempest. The latter also came with the company's very first inline-four engine. However, the brand's foray into this niche was short-lived; the Tempest became a mid-size car in 1964. While all the other Big Three divisions continued to offer compact cars, Pontiac opted out.
The story goes that GM prioritised the higher profit margins of the larger Pontiac models, leaving the cheaper compact segment to Chevrolet and its Chevy II/Nova. It was also a matter of protecting Pontiac's performance-oriented image. Instead of a traditional economy compact, Pontiac debuted the Firebird pony car as its smallest vehicle in 1967.
That changed in 1971 following the sudden collapse of the muscle car market. With the GTO no longer popular, GM gave Pontiac access to the X-body platform that had been underpinning the Chevy II/Nova since 1962 . The Ventura II was born. Additionally, both Buick and Oldsmobile introduced X-body compacts in 1973 (the Apollo and Omega, respectively).
The Ventura II was quite successful. The compact moved over 500,000 units through 1977, with record sales of 96,500 examples in 1973. Unsurprisingly given the high production numbers and low performance, the Ventura II is not a desirable classic today. However, this all-black 1972 coupe is definitely worth a closer look.
How so? Well, while it may look totally stock inside and out, this Ventura packs a beefed-up engine and a very long list of powertrain enhancements. The Poncho came standard with an inline-six in 1972, while the options list included two small-block V8 mills. The range-topping 350-cubic-inch (5.7-liter) powerplant delivered only 160 horsepower.
This Ventura was born with the latter based on the VIN, but the original V8 has been removed to make way for a nasty LSA-type unit . It's a supercharged 6.2-liter mill by Nickey Performance. There's no info on how powerful it is, but these Stage II engines delivered at least 600 horsepower.
All that oomph hits the rear wheels through a bespoke automatic transmission and a 10-bolt rear end with forged Moser axles and a Detroit locker. The list of upgrades also includes a Holley Terminator X engine management unit, an aluminium radiator with dual electric fans, and a custom cold air intake.
The Ventura also has stainless long-tube headers and mufflers, a race-spec driveshaft, adjustable shocks, front disc brakes, a CalTracs traction system, and a six-point roll bar. This Pontiac is ready to hit the drag strip and smoke any iconic muscle car from the golden era.
I found this Ventura while browsing the lots of Mecum's upcoming Las Vegas 2026 auction in November. It will cross the block on November 14, and it will probably become one of the most expensive compact Venturas ever sold at public auction.
